intro/hello: Welcome to Python and NumPy, the language of every assignment in this course.
intro/python: Python is the easy part: if you already program, an afternoon is enough.
intro/numpy: NumPy, its library for arrays of numbers, takes longer, and every line that does real work goes through it.
intro/loops: It asks you to stop thinking in loops, which visit one number at a time...
intro/whole: and to think in whole arrays instead, where one line touches every number at once.
intro/goal: By the end, a line like this one, which picks the correct class score for every example, should read as easily as a for loop.
intro/shape: And you should be able to predict the shape of every array before you print it.
python/x: Python has no type declarations. Write x equals three, and Python works out that x is a whole number.
python/div: One trap: a single slash always gives a decimal, so seven over two is three point five. Two slashes round down, to three.
python/pow: Two stars mean power, and the percent sign gives the remainder.
python/indent: There are no curly braces: the indentation is the block, and a colon starts one.
python/list: The workhorse container is the list, an ordered row of values, and counting starts at zero.
python/neg: Negative indices count back from the end: minus one is the last item.
python/slice: A slice picks a range. Picture indices as fence posts between items: one colon four takes what lies between posts one and four.
python/open: Leave out the start, and it begins at zero. Leave out the stop, and it runs to the end.
python/step: A third number is the step: two colons and a two take every second item.
python/comp: And a list comprehension builds a new list in one line: square each n, keeping only those above two.
python2/tuple: A tuple is a list in round brackets that cannot be changed. Unpack one into names, and px gets three, py gets four.
python2/dict: A dictionary maps keys to values. Ask for cat, and you get three.
python2/results: Assignment one stores its tuning results this way: a pair of settings as the key, a pair of accuracies as the value.
python2/def: Functions start with def, and an argument can have a default, like a leak of zero.
python2/kw: You can also pass arguments by name: a ray-loo of minus two, with a leak of zero point one, gives minus zero point two.
python2/cls: A class bundles data with the functions that use it. Every method takes self first: the object itself.
python2/new: Calling the class makes one, with no new keyword, and train just stores the data inside it.
python2/alias: Last, the habit that trips people up most: giving a list a second name does not copy it.
python2/same: Both names point at one list, so a change through either shows up in both. NumPy has its own version.
arrays/what: A NumPy array is a grid of numbers that all share one type, stored side by side in one block of memory.
arrays/fast: That is what makes it fast. A Python list points to objects scattered around memory, but an array is one tight block that NumPy loops over in compiled C.
arrays/v: Every array knows three things. Its shape is a tuple with one size per axis: this one has one axis, of length three.
arrays/ndim: Its ndim counts the axes. Its dtype is the type of every entry: here, whole numbers, int sixty four.
arrays/M: Rows of decimals make a two dimensional array. Axis zero runs down the rows, axis one across the columns.
arrays/Minfo: So its shape is two comma three, its ndim is two, and its dtype is float sixty four.
arrays/dtypes: Two more dtypes matter here: uint eight, for raw pixel values, and bool, for True and False.
arrays/make: NumPy also builds arrays for you: all zeros, all sevens, the identity, a range, evenly spaced points, or bell curve samples.
arrays/comma: One warning: the shape three comma, with its trailing comma, is a flat array. It is not a column, and not a row.
arrays/col: Three by one is a column and one by three is a row, both two dimensional. Mixing these up causes the most confusing bugs.
indexing/grid: Let us practice on a grid: the numbers zero to twenty three, poured into four rows of six.
indexing/one: Indexing takes one index per axis, separated by commas. Row one, column three, is the number nine.
indexing/row: An axis you leave out means all of it, so a single index, two, gives the whole of row two.
indexing/col: For a column, write a bare colon for the rows, meaning all of them, then zero.
indexing/flat: But what comes back is a flat row of four numbers, shape four comma. Not a column.
indexing/drop: That is the rule: an integer index removes its axis, a slice keeps it. Columns zero up to one give four by one.
indexing/block: Slices on both axes cut out a block: rows one up to three, columns two up to five, a two by three piece.
indexing/step: Steps work too, like every second row and every third column. And minus one is the last row.
indexing/view: One more thing: a slice copies nothing. It is a view, a window onto the same memory.
indexing/write: So writing into the view writes into the original: the alias trap again, and why slicing is so fast.
picking/ints: Now a power move: you can index an axis with a whole array of integers.
picking/setup: Here is why. Scores has a row per example and a column per class, and the loss needs one cell per row: the correct class, which y holds.
picking/rows: n p dot arange of N gives the row numbers, and y gives one column for each row.
picking/pick: Index with both, and NumPy pairs them up like zip: row zero with column two, row one with column zero, and so on.
picking/one: One score per example, in one line. The vectorized SVM and softmax losses both lean on it.
picking/wrong: The classic mistake is a colon for the rows: it takes every row at every label, a five by five array, and gives a silently wrong loss.
picking/write: The same trick writes, too: this zeroes every row's correct-class entry at once.
picking/mask: Masks are the other fancy index. Compare an array with something, and you get booleans of the same shape.
picking/sel: Index with the mask, and you get the True entries, as a flat copy.
picking/and: Combine conditions with ampersand, bar and tilde, wrapping each comparison in parentheses; and, or and not fail on arrays.
picking/relu: Assigning through a mask changes only those positions: zeroing every negative entry is a ray-loo.
picking/acc: And the mean of a boolean array is the fraction that are True: accuracy.
math/elem: Arithmetic on arrays works entry by entry: plus, times, even greater than all pair up matching entries.
math/mul: So A times A squares every entry: one, four, nine, sixteen.
math/ufunc: NumPy's math functions, like square root, exp and log, also run on every entry at once.
math/mat: The matrix product is different, spelled with the at sign: each entry is a row dotted with a column. One times one, plus two times three, is seven.
math/bug: Mixing them up is a classic bug that often does not crash: for square matrices, both are legal.
math/relu: The course uses both: X dot W for scores, and the star to zero a ray-loo's gradient wherever its input was negative.
math/reduce: Reductions collapse an array: sum, mean, max, argmax. With no arguments they collapse everything: this grid sums to thirty five.
math/ax0: With axis equals zero, the rows collapse: each column slides down into one number.
math/ax1: With axis equals one, the columns collapse, leaving one number per row.
math/rule: So, the axis you name is the one that disappears: three by four, summed over axis one, is three comma.
math/keep: With keepdims equals True, the collapsed axis stays, with size one: three by one, still lined up with the original.
math/argmax: And argmax reports where each winner sits: the column of each row's biggest score, which is how a classifier picks its label.
broadcasting/q: What happens when you add two arrays of different shapes? Often, exactly what you meant.
broadcasting/ex: Add a row of four numbers to a three by four grid, and the row is added to every row of the grid.
broadcasting/stretch: This is broadcasting: NumPy acts as if the smaller array were stretched to match, copying nothing.
broadcasting/r1: The rules: line the shapes up from the right, and pad the shorter one on the left with ones.
broadcasting/r2: Then, axis by axis, equal sizes are fine, and a size of one is stretched to match.
broadcasting/outer: Both can stretch at once: a column of three times a row of four makes a whole multiplication table.
broadcasting/bad: Anything else fails. Three numbers against a three by four grid: from the right, three meets four, and NumPy refuses.
broadcasting/bias: The course uses this everywhere. Scores are N by C, the biases just C, so every example gets the same biases.
broadcasting/center: Centering subtracts the mean image, shape D, from each of the N images.
broadcasting/norm: And dividing each row by its sum makes probabilities: with keepdims, the sums are N by one, so each stretches across its row.
distances/task: Now broadcasting does real work: the distance from every test image to every training image, with no loops.
distances/table: With N test images and M training images, that is an N by M table, one distance per pair.
distances/square: The trick is school algebra: x minus t, squared, is x squared, minus two x t, plus t squared.
distances/vec: For vectors it reads: the squared length of x, minus twice x dot t, plus the squared length of t.
distances/x2: Each term works for all pairs at once. The test images' squared lengths form a column, N by one.
distances/t2: The training images' squared lengths form a row of M.
distances/cross: And every test image dotted with every training image is one matrix product, N by M.
distances/glue: Broadcasting glues them: the column stretches across, the row stretches down, and all three line up as N by M.
distances/clip: Rounding can push a tiny squared distance below zero, so clip at zero before the square root.
reshape/reshape: Reshape gives the same numbers a new shape. Nothing moves in memory; only the reading changes.
reshape/order: NumPy reads in row-major order, along each row and then down, like a book, and pours into the new shape the same way.
reshape/minus: The count cannot change, so minus one means work it out: six numbers in three rows makes two columns.
reshape/T: Transpose is different: it swaps the axes, so rows become columns.
reshape/img: Now images. The assignments load each see-far ten image as thirty two by thirty two by three: height, width, channels, called H W C.
reshape/px: A row and a column pick out one pixel: its red, green and blue values.
reshape/flat: A linear classifier wants each image as one long vector, and row-major order decides where each value lands.
reshape/hwc: The last axis changes fastest. In H W C that is the channel, so the vector runs red, green, blue, red, green, blue.
reshape/chw: Assignment two's convolution layers put channels first, C H W. Flattened, that gives all the reds, then all the greens, then all the blues.
reshape/same: Either works if every image uses the same one; mixing them scrambles your data. A batch becomes one N by three thousand and seventy two matrix.
vectorize/speed: Why think in whole arrays? Speed. Python is interpreted, and every pass through a loop pays for bookkeeping.
vectorize/loop: Adding up a million numbers in a Python loop takes about fifty milliseconds.
vectorize/np: n p dot sum hands the whole loop to compiled code: about zero point one five milliseconds, over three hundred times faster.
vectorize/rule: So the rule for fast code is short: keep the loops out of Python.
vectorize/two: Assignment one makes you feel it. With two loops, Python takes one step per pair of images.
vectorize/one: With one loop, each step fills a whole row.
vectorize/zero: With no loops, there is one step: the distance trick, its work in one matrix multiply.
vectorize/sizes: At the assignment's sizes: two and a half million steps, five hundred, or one. About six seconds, five seconds, and four hundredths of a second.
vectorize/why: One loop barely helps, because each step still builds a huge temporary array.
vectorize/how: To vectorize, think in shapes, not indices: write down every input's shape and the answer's, then find the operations that connect them.
vectorize/check: And check the fast version against the slow loop on a small input, with n p dot all close.
pitfalls/three: Before we wrap up, three pitfalls that catch almost everyone. First, views.
pitfalls/view: A slice is a window, so writing into the slice writes into the original.
pitfalls/copy: To change an array you were handed, copy it first. Integer and mask indexing always copy.
pitfalls/int: Second, dtypes. Store zero point nine in an integer array, and it silently becomes zero.
pitfalls/u8: Images arrive as uint eight, whole numbers up to two hundred and fifty five: two hundred plus two hundred wraps, like an odometer, to one hundred and forty four.
pitfalls/fix: So convert to floats before any arithmetic, as the assignment's loader does.
pitfalls/flat: Third, the nastiest: a flat shape, three comma, against a column, three by one. Transposing the flat one does nothing.
pitfalls/trap: Add them, and broadcasting stretches both: you expected three numbers and got a three by three table, with no error.
pitfalls/assert: The cure is cheap: when a shape surprises you, print it, and assert shapes throughout your code.
outro/plt: One last tool: matplotlib, which draws the assignments' loss curves and image grids.
outro/plot: plt dot plot draws a curve through x and y values: here a ray-loo and a tan h.
outro/loss: Give it one array, and it plots each value against its position: a training curve.
outro/img: im show draws an H W C image with whole numbers up to two hundred and fifty five, hence the cast to uint eight. And subplot makes a grid.
outro/recap1: That is the toolkit. Every array has a shape: predict it. Integers drop their axis, slices keep it, and slices are views.
outro/recap2: Star is elementwise, at is the matrix product, the axis you name disappears, and broadcasting stretches the ones.
outro/recap3: And Python loops are slow: vectorize, then check against the loop.
outro/next: Next comes image classification, where these arrays become real photos, and one vectorized line compares them all at once.
